slides.title: Detailed Lifecycle Stages: Processes & Environmental Impacts
slides.text:
(Extracting) Raw materials
• This step involves digging for basic metal and oil start materials using techniques like big furnaces or electricity.
• Digging leads to habitat loss, fewer types of animals and plants, and changes the land forever.
• Basic starting materials (like raw metal or oil) are found from the ground, sea, or air.

Manufacture and distribution
• This is the process of putting basic parts together to make final products, often with robots.
• Factories turn raw plastics and metals into things like bottles or phones.
• Making and shipping products uses a huge amount of energy and fuel.

Using the product
• This stage is when the customer actually uses the product during its life.
• Products like phones and electric cars need constant electricity to work, using power over years.
• The less often you replace a product, the less total energy and materials you use.

Disposal
• Rubbish dumps use up useful space on the planet for many centuries.
• This step is when you get rid of a product that is broken or no longer useful.
• Materials are sorted into household recycling bins, rubbish dumps, or sent to be burned.
• Harmful chemicals can seep into the soil and pollute nearby water.
• Burning materials releases dirty air into the atmosphere.

slides.title: OCR Exam Checkpoint: 6-Mark LCA Evaluation (Plastic Packet vs Metal Can)
slides.text:
1. A life-cycle assessment looks at the potential environmental impact at each stage of the life of a product.
Cat food is sold in plastic packets or metal cans.
The table shows information about these two containers:
• Raw Materials: Plastic packet (Crude oil) vs Metal can (Aluminium ore)
• Manufacture: Plastic packet (Fractional distillation, Cracking, Polymerisation) vs Metal can (Aluminium ore is mined, Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis)
• Using the product: Plastic packet (Usually single use) vs Metal can (Usually single use but easily repurposed or upcycled)
• Disposal of the product: Plastic packet (Harder to recycle, Not biodegradable so takes up space in landfill, 90% energy saved by recycling) vs Metal can (Easier to recycle, Not biodegradable so takes up space in landfill, 95% energy saved by recycling)
Evaluate which type of container has the smallest environmental impact over its lifetime.
Use the information in the table, and your own scientific knowledge. [6 marks]
